paragraphs: I have now nearly reached the end of my inquiry. Up to this point, in speaking of the future of the United States, I have tried to divide my subject into distinct parts so that I could study each with more attention. My aim now is to take in the whole from a single point of view. My remarks will be less detailed, but they will be more reliable. I shall see each object less distinctly, but I shall make out the principal facts with more certainty. A traveler who has just left the walls of an immense city climbs the neighboring hill. As he goes farther away, he loses sight of the people he has just left. Their dwellings blur into a dense mass; he can no longer distinguish the public squares, and he can scarcely trace the great thoroughfares. But his eye has less difficulty following the boundaries of the city, and for the first time he sees the shape of the vast whole. That is how the future of the British race in North America appears to me. The details of the stupendous picture are lost in shadow, but I form a clear idea of the whole subject.

The territory the United States of America now occupies or possesses makes up about one-twentieth of the habitable earth. But extensive as these boundaries are, we must not suppose that the Anglo-American race will always remain within them. Indeed, it has already gone far beyond them.

There was once a time when we too might have created a great French nation in the American wilds, to counterbalance the influence of the English on the destinies of the New World. France formerly held a territory in North America scarcely smaller than the whole of Europe. The three greatest rivers of that continent then flowed through her dominions. The Native American tribes living between the mouth of the St. Lawrence and the delta of the Mississippi knew no tongue but ours, and all the European settlements scattered across that immense region recalled the traditions of our country. Louisbourg, Montmorency, Duquesne, St. Louis, Vincennes, New Orleans (for such were the names they bore) are words dear to France and familiar to our ears.

But a combination of circumstances, which it would be tedious to list, *m has deprived us of this magnificent inheritance. Wherever the French settlers were few in number and only partly established, they have disappeared. Those who remain are gathered in a small stretch of country and are now subject to other laws. The 400,000 French inhabitants of Lower Canada are at present the remnant of an old nation lost in the midst of a new people. A foreign population is growing around them ceaselessly and on every side. It already penetrates among the ancient masters of the country, predominates in their cities, and corrupts their language. This population is identical with that of the United States. I was therefore right to say that the British race is not confined within the frontiers of the Union, since it already extends to the northeast.

m [ The foremost of these circumstances is that nations accustomed to free institutions and municipal government are better able than any others to found prosperous colonies. The habit of thinking and governing for oneself is indispensable in a new country, where success necessarily depends, to a great extent, on the individual efforts of the settlers.]

To the northwest there is nothing but a few insignificant Russian settlements, but to the southwest Mexico presents a barrier to the Anglo-Americans. Thus the Spaniards and the Anglo-Americans are, strictly speaking, the only two races that divide possession of the New World. The boundary between them has been fixed by treaty. But although the terms of that treaty are exceedingly favorable to the Anglo-Americans, I have no doubt that they will soon break it. Vast provinces beyond the frontiers of the Union, toward Mexico, are still without inhabitants. The natives of the United States will get ahead of the rightful occupants of these solitary regions. They will take possession of the soil and establish social institutions, so that when the legal owner finally arrives, he will find the wilderness under cultivation and strangers quietly settled in the middle of his inheritance. *n
n [ [This was quickly accomplished, and before long both Texas and California formed part of the United States. The Russian settlements were acquired by purchase.]]

The lands of the New World belong to the first occupant, and they are the natural reward of the swiftest pioneer. Even the countries that are already settled will have some difficulty protecting themselves from this invasion. I have already mentioned what is happening in the province of Texas. Inhabitants of the United States are constantly migrating to Texas, where they buy land. Although they obey the laws of the country, they are gradually founding the empire of their own language and their own customs. The province of Texas is still part of the Mexican dominions, but it will soon contain no Mexicans. The same thing has happened whenever the Anglo-Americans have come into contact with populations of a different origin.

It cannot be denied that the British race has gained an amazing preponderance over all the other European races in the New World, and that it is very superior to them in civilization, in industry, and in power. As long as it is surrounded only by desert or thinly populated countries, and meets no dense populations on its route that it cannot work its way through, it will certainly continue to spread. The lines drawn by treaties will not stop it; it will cross these imaginary barriers everywhere.

The geographical position of the British race in the New World is especially favorable to its rapid increase. Above its northern frontiers lie the icy regions of the Pole, and a few degrees below its southern limits lies the burning climate of the Equator. The Anglo-Americans are therefore placed in the most temperate and habitable zone of the continent.

It is generally supposed that the prodigious growth of population in the United States came after the Declaration of Independence. But this is an error. The population increased as rapidly under the colonial system as it does today; that is, it doubled in about twenty-two years. But this proportion, which is now applied to millions, was then applied to thousands of inhabitants, and the same fact that was scarcely noticeable a century ago is now evident to every observer.

The British subjects in Canada, who are dependent on a king, increase and spread almost as rapidly as the British settlers of the United States, who live under a republican government. During the War of Independence, which lasted eight years, the population continued to increase at the same rate without interruption. Although powerful Native American nations allied with the English then existed on the western frontiers, emigration westward was never checked. While the enemy laid waste the shores of the Atlantic, Kentucky, the western parts of Pennsylvania, and the States of Vermont and Maine were filling with inhabitants. Nor did the unsettled state of the Constitution that followed the war prevent the population from growing or stop its progress across the wilds. Thus the differences of laws, the varying conditions of peace and war, of order and anarchy, have had no perceptible influence on the gradual development of the Anglo-Americans. This is easy to understand, for no causes are general enough to exert a simultaneous influence over the whole of so extensive a territory. One part of the country always offers a sure refuge from the calamities that afflict another part, and however great the evil may be, the remedy at hand is greater still.

It must not be imagined, then, that the impulse of the British race in the New World can be halted. The dismemberment of the Union and the hostilities that might ensue, the abolition of republican institutions and the tyrannical government that might follow, may slow this impulse, but they cannot keep it from ultimately fulfilling the destinies reserved for that race. No power on earth can close to the emigrants that fertile wilderness, which offers resources to all industry and a refuge from all want. Future events, of whatever nature, will not deprive the Americans of their climate or their inland seas, their great rivers or their exuberant soil. Nor will bad laws, revolutions, and anarchy be able to wipe out the love of prosperity and the spirit of enterprise that seem to be the distinctive characteristics of their race, or to extinguish the knowledge that guides them on their way.

Thus, in the midst of an uncertain future, one event at least is sure. At a time that may be called near (for we are speaking of the life of a nation), the Anglo-Americans alone will cover the immense space between the polar regions and the tropics, extending from the coasts of the Atlantic to the shores of the Pacific Ocean. The territory the Anglo-Americans will probably occupy at some future time may be reckoned as equal to three-quarters of Europe in extent. *o The climate of the Union is on the whole better than that of Europe, and its natural advantages are no less great. It is therefore clear that its population will at some future time be proportionate to our own. Europe, divided as it is among so many different nations and torn as it has been by incessant wars and the barbarous customs of the Middle Ages, has nevertheless reached a population of 410 inhabitants to the square league. *p What cause can prevent the United States from having as numerous a population in time?

o [ The United States already extend over a territory equal to one-half of Europe. The area of Europe is 500,000 square leagues, and its population 205,000,000 inhabitants. (“Malte Brun,” liv. 114. vol. vi. p. 4.)

[This calculation is given in French leagues, which were in use when the author was writing. Twenty years later, in 1850, the surface area of the United States had grown to 3,306,865 square miles of territory, which is about the area of Europe.]]
p [ See “Malte Brun,” liv. 116, vol. vi. p. 92.]

Many ages must pass before the various offshoots of the British race in America cease to show the same homogeneous characteristics, and the time cannot be foreseen when a permanent inequality of conditions will be established in the New World. Whatever differences may arise from peace or war, from freedom or oppression, from prosperity or want, between the destinies of the different descendants of the great Anglo-American family, they will at least keep a similar social condition, and they will share the customs and opinions that this social condition has produced.

In the Middle Ages, the tie of religion was powerful enough to give all the different populations of Europe the same civilization. The British of the New World have a thousand other mutual ties, and they live at a time when the tendency toward equality is general among mankind. The Middle Ages were a period when everything was broken up, when each people, each province, each city, and each family had a strong tendency to preserve its distinct individuality. At the present time an opposite tendency seems to prevail, and the nations seem to be advancing toward unity. Our means of intellectual exchange link the most remote parts of the earth, and it is impossible for people to remain strangers to each other or to be ignorant of the events taking place in any corner of the globe. The result is that there is less difference today between the Europeans and their descendants in the New World than there was in the thirteenth century between certain towns separated only by a river. If this tendency toward assimilation brings foreign nations closer to each other, it must all the more prevent the descendants of the same people from becoming aliens to each other.

The time will therefore come when one hundred and fifty million people will be living in North America, *q equal in condition, the offspring of one race, owing their origin to the same cause, and preserving the same civilization, the same language, the same religion, the same habits, and the same customs, and imbued with the same opinions, spread in the same forms. The rest is uncertain, but this is certain. And it is a fact new to the world — a fact so full of momentous consequences that it defeats even the efforts of the imagination.
q [ This would be a population proportionate to that of Europe, taken at an average rate of 410 inhabitants to the square league.]

At the present time there are two great nations in the world that seem to be tending toward the same end, although they started from different points. I mean the Russians and the Americans. Both have grown up unnoticed, and while the attention of mankind was directed elsewhere, they have suddenly taken a most prominent place among the nations. The world learned of their existence and their greatness at almost the same time.

All other nations seem to have nearly reached their natural limits and to be charged only with maintaining their power, but these two are still growing. *r All the others are stopped, or continue to advance with extreme difficulty; these are proceeding with ease and speed along a path to which the human eye can assign no end. The American struggles against the natural obstacles that oppose him; the Russian’s adversaries are men. The former combats the wilderness and savage life; the latter, civilization with all its weapons and its arts. The conquests of the one are therefore won with the plowshare, those of the other with the sword. The Anglo-American relies on personal interest to accomplish his ends and gives free scope to the unguided efforts and common sense of the citizens. The Russian concentrates all the authority of society in a single arm. The principal instrument of the former is freedom; of the latter, servitude. Their starting points are different and their courses are not the same; yet each of them seems marked out by the will of Heaven to sway the destinies of half the globe.
r [ Russia is the country in the Old World where population increases most rapidly in proportion.]
